abstract:
Recent
advances in the sensitivity and speed of mass spectrometers
coupled with improved sample preparation methods have enabled the
field of single cell proteomics to proliferate. While heavy development
is occurring in the label free space, dramatic improvements in throughput
are provided by multiplexing with tandem mass tags. Hundreds or thousands
of single cells can be analyzed with this method, yielding large data
sets which may contain poor data arising from loss of material during
cell sorting or poor digestion, labeling, and lysis. To date, no tools
have been described that can assess data quality prior to data processing.
We present herein a lightweight python script and accompanying graphic
user interface that can rapidly quantify reporter ion peaks within
each MS/MS spectrum in a file. With simple summary reports, we can
identify single cell samples that fail to pass a set quality threshold,
thus reducing analysis time waste. In addition, this tool, Diagnostic
Ion Data Analysis Reduction (DIDAR), will create reduced MGF files
containing only spectra possessing a user-specified number of single
cell reporter ions. By reducing the number of spectra that have excessive
zero values, we can speed up sample processing with little loss in
data completeness as these spectra are removed in later stages in
data processing workflows. DIDAR and the DIDAR GUI are compatible
with all modern operating systems and are available at: https://github.com/orsburn/DIDARSCPQC . All files described in this study are available at www.massive.ucsd.edu as accession
MSV000088887.

Methods
and Materials
Script Development
DIDAR was written
in Python 3.8
using Spyder 4.1.4. IDE.
14
DIDAR is contained
in less than 100 total lines of code, inclusive of comments and line
spacing. In addition, utilizing the built-in os python package as
the only dependency adds to the lightweight nature of the program.
The DIDAR graphical user interface (GUI) was constructed by using
the tkinter python package as a shell to directly execute the original
script. The DIDARSCPGUI program was designed to be directly executable
on any Windows PC by unzipping the V1.0.3 or newer folder and double
clicking on the DIDARSCPGUI.py program. The program has been tested
for compatibility with Windows 7, 10, and 11. For MacIntosh, it is
necessary to execute the .py file through an IDE program. Links to
instructional videos have been made available, and all scripts and
example files are available at:
https://github.com/orsburn/DIDARSCPQC
.
Single Cell Proteomics by Mass Spectrometry (SCoPE-MS) Data
Quality Filtering
For the development of DIDAR, we used publicly
available files from two recent SCoPE-MS studies. The first utilized
the 9 unit resolution mass tags from the TMTPro16 reagents to study
single human KRAS
G12C
model cells (NCI-H-358) using a third-generation
TIMSTOF mass analyzer with 30 min acquisitions.
15
We will refer to this as Study A. Due to challenges inherent
in working in the Bruker .d multilevel file format, the vendor format
instrument files from each study were converted to MGF using MSConvert
Version: 3.0.20310-0d96039e2 (developer build) using the default conversions
for each instrument. The reporter ion region of each MS/MS spectra
was recalibrated using the exact mass of the 134 reporter ion as reference
as described previously.
15
For verifying
compatibility with SCoPE-MS data from Thermo instruments, we used
the publicly available files from the SCOPE2 study. This study details
the use of both TMT11-plex and TMTPro16-plex tags to study macrophage
heterogeneity using a quadrupole Orbitrap MS2 based approach with
95 min acquisition times.
2
For the remainder
of this article, we will refer to this as Study B.
For applying
DIDAR to SCoPE-MS files, the DIDAR.py and diagnostic
ion text list were copied into the folder containing the MGF files
from each respective study. The diagnostic ion text file referenced
by DIDAR contained only the exact masses of the reporter ions as
reported by the manufacturer. The DIDAR script was executed identically
for each file, with the exception of the ion mass tolerance, which
was set at 0.005 Da for the Orbitrap files in Study A and 0.002 Da
for the TIMSTOF files in Study B to compensate for the relative differences
in mass accuracy between these analyzers. To obtain measurements of
the number of spectra with a signal in the method blank (126) channel,
files were analyzed with DIDAR using the completed list of reporter
ions used in the experiment. Figures were generated from the DIDAR
Diagnostic.txt files summarized in GraphPad Prism 9.
Comparison
of Filtered Data to Original Files
For comparison
of filtering effects on proteomic data, 45 files containing approximately
270 single cells from Study A were used, which compared control and
sotorasib treated single cells. The 45 files were processed in both
completed and DIDAR filtered form with identical parameters in Proteome
Discoverer 2.4 using the SequestHT search engine with Percolator rescoring.
16
Briefly, all files were processed against the
UniProt/SwissProt Human database downloaded on 11/10/2021 and the
cRAP (
www.gpm.org
) contaminant
library, downloaded on 3/1/2021. A 15 ppm MS1 tolerance and 0.05 Da
MS/MS tolerance were used for all searches. Oxidation of methionine,
phosphorylation of serine and threonine and acetylation, and methylation
and dimethylation of lysine were considered as dynamic modifications
in addition to the TMTPro tags. The TMTPro reagent mass was set as
static for all of the peptide N-termini. The same files were reduced
using DIDAR in which a minimum of 2 reporter ions within 0.005 Da
from the 127n, 128n, 129n, 130n, 131n, 132n, or 133n single cell TMTPro
channels. As the carrier channel in these files was the 134n and the
method blank control was the 126 channel, signals within the range
of these reporters were not used for DIDAR file reduction. The original
MGFs and filtered MGFs were analyzed by using the same pipeline in
Proteome Discoverer 2.4. For quantification, the commercial reporter
ion workflow was employed by using the default settings provided by
the vendor for Q Exactive reporter ion quantification with minor alterations.
First, only unique peptides were used for quantification, and “unique”
was determined at the protein, rather than the protein group level.
Finally, a sum-based normalization strategy was used so that the total
reporter ion signal from each single cell was effectively equal.
Data Availability Statement
All original files used
in this study are publicly available on the MASSIVE repository (massive.ucsd.edu).
The SCOPE2 quadrupole Orbitrap files are available as accessions MSV000083945
and MSV000084660. The TIMSTOF single cell files were accessed as accessions
MSV000088144. All DIDAR filtered MGFs and output metrics for this
study have been deposited at:
ftp://massive.ucsd.edu/MSV000088887/
.
Code Availability Statement
The DIDAR script and diagnostic
ion text files for TMT reporter ions and a video tutorial for using
the tool are available at:
https://github.com/orsburn/DIDARSCPQC
. A simplified streamlined version of DIDAR with a graphical user
interface (DIDARSCPGUI) has been deposited at this GitHub as well.
DIDARSCPGUI features single click installation on any Windows PC.
A tutorial video on the site explains installation and operation on
both Windows and MacIntosh PCs.

Introduction
Single cell proteomics by mass spectrometry
is an emerging field
of research largely made possible by the innovative reuse of existing
technology. The revolutionary work of Budnik et al., first described
the SCoPE-MS workflow whereby the additive signal of multiplexed peptide
samples could be leveraged to effectively amplify peptide signal from
single cells.
1
To achieve these effects,
SCoPE-MS employs a carrier channel of isobarically labeled peptides
of higher relative concentration to resuspend labeled peptides from
single cells. Data dependent LCMS analysis of these multiplexed samples
leads to the fragmentation and identification of peptides from the
carrier channel. The isobaric reporter ion fragments corresponding
to labels applied to single cells, if within the intrascan linear
dynamic range of the instrument, can be used for assigning both peptide
identification and quantification to the cells themselves.
2
−
5
Although other single cell technologies such as single cell RNaseq
have been sorting and analyzing single cells for over a decade with
increasingly sophisticated technology, relatively little of this can
be applied to proteomics approaches.
6
,
7
New technologies
such as nanoPOTs,
8
nPOP,
4
LevCell
9
and ProteoChip
5
are improving reproducible peptide recovery from
cells, however technical challenges in sample preparation may be the
biggest limiter to entry into single cell proteomics today. Single
human cells and the volumes of reagents used in their preparation
and analysis can be affected by factors as ubiquitous as relative
humidity and static electricity.
10
As a
relatively large number of single cells must be analyzed for sufficient
statistics to capture both technical and biological variability, failed
runs may not be detected until final data analysis, which may take
days or weeks to complete. Multiple high likelihood failure points
in multiplexed SCP workflows have been identified by our laboratories
and others in the SCP community.
11
A single
cell in a multiplexed set may fail due to the cell being incorrectly
aliquoted, leading to the cell adhering to an improper location in
the reaction well or simply not reaching the well entirely. In both
cases, lysis and digestion will not occur, thus leading to an empty
multiplex channel and loss of data points. A more severe failure is
when an entire multiplex injection fails. This can arise from LC pickup
issues, incorrectly prepared carrier channels, or other standard
LCMS quality issues. The final, and most detrimental, situation would
be if an entire plate of cells were to fail due to issues such as
a plate miscalibration during single cell aliquoting.
3
,
4
,
12
,
13
In this case, each plate may require additional dozens or hundreds
of hours to run and process, which is a major setback for a project.
Quality control tools that could be leveraged prior to complete data
analysis could simplify and improve nearly all of the downstream processes.
Methods
and Materials
Script Development
DIDAR was written
in Python 3.8
using Spyder 4.1.4. IDE.
14
DIDAR is contained
in less than 100 total lines of code, inclusive of comments and line
spacing. In addition, utilizing the built-in os python package as
the only dependency adds to the lightweight nature of the program.
The DIDAR graphical user interface (GUI) was constructed by using
the tkinter python package as a shell to directly execute the original
script. The DIDARSCPGUI program was designed to be directly executable
on any Windows PC by unzipping the V1.0.3 or newer folder and double
clicking on the DIDARSCPGUI.py program. The program has been tested
for compatibility with Windows 7, 10, and 11. For MacIntosh, it is
necessary to execute the .py file through an IDE program. Links to
instructional videos have been made available, and all scripts and
example files are available at:
https://github.com/orsburn/DIDARSCPQC
.
Single Cell Proteomics by Mass Spectrometry (SCoPE-MS) Data
Quality Filtering
For the development of DIDAR, we used publicly
available files from two recent SCoPE-MS studies. The first utilized
the 9 unit resolution mass tags from the TMTPro16 reagents to study

G12C
model cells (NCI-H-358) using a third-generation

Version: 3.0.20310-0d96039e2 (developer build) using the default conversions
for each instrument. The reporter ion region of each MS/MS spectra

15

heterogeneity using a quadrupole Orbitrap MS2 based approach with

2

of this article, we will refer to this as Study B.
For applying
DIDAR to SCoPE-MS files, the DIDAR.py and diagnostic
ion text list were copied into the folder containing the MGF files
from each respective study. The diagnostic ion text file referenced

of Filtered Data to Original Files
For comparison
of filtering effects on proteomic data, 45 files containing approximately
270 single cells from Study A were used, which compared control and

16
Briefly, all files were processed against the
UniProt/SwissProt Human database downloaded on 11/10/2021 and the
cRAP (
www.gpm.org
) contaminant
library, downloaded on 3/1/2021. A 15 ppm MS1 tolerance and 0.05 Da

Data Availability Statement
All original files used
in this study are publicly available on the MASSIVE repository (massive.ucsd.edu).
The SCOPE2 quadrupole Orbitrap files are available as accessions MSV000083945
and MSV000084660. The TIMSTOF single cell files were accessed as accessions
MSV000088144. All DIDAR filtered MGFs and output metrics for this
study have been deposited at:
ftp://massive.ucsd.edu/MSV000088887/
.
Code Availability Statement
The DIDAR script and diagnostic
ion text files for TMT reporter ions and a video tutorial for using
the tool are available at:
https://github.com/orsburn/DIDARSCPQC
. A simplified streamlined version of DIDAR with a graphical user
interface (DIDARSCPGUI) has been deposited at this GitHub as well.
DIDARSCPGUI features single click installation on any Windows PC.
A tutorial video on the site explains installation and operation on
both Windows and MacIntosh PCs.
Results and Discussion
DIDAR
Provides Quality Assurance Readout of SCP Data
Each file
processed through DIDAR produced two output files. The
first is a new filtered MGF containing only spectra meeting the end
user’s criteria. For example, by changing the minimum number
of reporter ions to 5, we will create an output file that only contains
spectra where at least 5 of the user defined TMT reporter ions are
observed. The second output file is a small diagnostic text file that
provides a simple count of the number of spectra in which each diagnostic
ion is counted. The diagnostic file can provide preprocessing metrics
of batch qualities.
Figure
1
A is a summary of the DIDAR output from a batch of 25 files
from Study A. For ease of visualization, we included the 126 method
blank control channel, and we did not include the 134 channel which,
in this study, was the carrier channel. As previously reported by
others, isotopic impurities can lead to inflation of the reporter
ion signal in the lanes closest to the carrier channel.
17
,
18
This can be observed in the cells labeled with 133 which have dramatically
higher counts than the other single cell lanes. In addition, an excessive
signal in the method blank control channel, 126, can be observed in
one LCMS run by the data point at nearly the mean for the single cell
lanes. Finally, a single cell labeled with 131 is observed, which
has over 4 times the average number of counts as any single cell.
This rapid preprocessing analysis indicates that one LCMS run may
need to be discarded prior to analysis for contamination in the blank
channel, a single cell which may need flagged for contamination, and
indicates that all cells labeled with 133n should be discarded from
quantitative analysis.
Figure 1
Two use cases for DIDAR as a preprocess quality assurance
tool.
(A) Summary of the number of reporter ions observed in a batch of
25 multiplexed cells. (B) Focused analysis of the number of counts
of cells labeled with the 128n reagent across a batch of cells indicates
two files (775 and 782) that should be further evaluated.
DIDAR Can Rapidly Identify Cells That Failed
As mentioned
previously, there are multiple reasons why you will not get good data
from a single cell. In addition, entire LCMS runs or plates of cells
can also fail.
Figure
1
B is an example use case of a focused search to identify the original
RAW files for failed cells across a batch of LCMS injections. The
x
-axis represents the vendor RAW file labeling format in
which each run performed on the instrument is assigned a unique sequential
identifier by default for every file from instrument installation
onward. This focused plot can be easily extracted from the DIDAR output
text files to identify the original cells with technical issues. Both
RAW files 775 and 782 have substantially fewer spectra demonstrating
counts of the 128n reporter ion than the typical file, suggesting
that further investigation is necessary. When evaluating the original
diagnostic counts output data summarized (
Supplemental Data 1
) we see that in run 782 the failure was comprehensive
for the LCMS injection as no reporter ion for a single cell reported
more than 1,500 spectra with observed reporter ion signal. In contrast,
run 775 appears to have a near average number of reporter ions in
all measured channels except the cell labeled with 128n, suggesting
that a technical issue occurred in the handling or processing of that
single cell. While multiple groups have now reported on the use of
picoliter robotics systems capable of photographing and measuring
each cell as it is being deposited, obtaining this system may be a
financial challenge for many laboratories.
5
,
12
Even
when using the CellenOne system, we have found it both challenging
and time-consuming to look through each photograph of each cell. In
addition, this photograph only tells us that a cell was isolated.
It does not provide information about lysis or digestion efficiency.
DIDAR allows us to trace back to the original cell with a failure
and to sort through just a few photographs to determine if that cell
was present during aliquoting or whether an issue occurred following
aliquoting. Similarly, a significantly lower cost system was recently
described which does not possess imaging capabilities.
19
This aliquoting device does, however, record
resistance across the cellular membrane as a quality assurance metric.
Our laboratories now have both of these systems, and we envision DIDAR
as one step in a comprehensive quality assurance pipeline to determine
that single cell data is not being acquired. In conjunction with other
tools, we can then identify the source of these issues whether they
are occurring during cell aliquoting, lysis, digestion, and labeling
or due to LCMS issues to improve both data quality and data gathering
efficiency.
Assessing DIDAR Effects on Proteomic Data
To assess
the impact DIDAR reduction and filtering has on identified proteins,
we selected 45 files from Study A containing the multiplexed results
of 270 single human cancer cells. Identical processing was performed
on both the original and the DIDAR filtered files. As shown in
Figure
2
, DIDAR filtering
resulted in a loss of approximately 10% of the identified proteins
groups. The effect was more dramatic at the peptide group level as
filtering reduced the number of identified peptides from 17,832 to
14,936 (16.2%). The most dramatic decrease was at the peptide spectral
match level, where 45.7% of peptide spectral matches were removed
during the filtering process. However, the filtering process appeared
to have minimal detrimental effects on the accuracy of protein identifications
as only 37 of 2,341 proteins were identified exclusively in the DIDAR
filtered files (1.4%). To assess the quantitative impact of removing
spectra without confident reporter ion signals, we compared the %
CV of each identified protein in the original and DIDAR filtered files.
As shown in
Figure
2
B, we observe a substantial reduction in the CV% of the protein group
level, which we believe is due to the removal of over 1.88 million
MS/MS spectra that contained no reporter ion signal. It is also worth
noting that the DIDAR filtered files can be processed on the same
PC by using the same workflow in approximately 30% of the amount of
time necessary for the unfiltered files. The complete protein identifications
are provided in
Supplemental Data 1
. For
full evaluation of the results following filtering, MS2GO reports
containing all protein, peptide, and PSMS were created from these
analyses and deposited at FigShare and published at DOI:
10.6084/m9.figshare.21330465
.
Figure 2
Comparison of the analysis of raw output single cell data compared
to DIDAR filtered files. (A) Protein identifications resulting from
unfiltered files (blue) and DIDAR filtered files (gray) from 270 cells
from a recent SCoPE-MS study. (A) Density plot displaying the distribution
of protein %CVs in the unfiltered files (gray) and DIDAR filtered
files (blue).
While there is intrinsic variability
in protein abundance measurements
resulting from both technical challenges and valid biological variability,
we find the reduction in %CV for each protein group following the
removal of spectra with no single cell signal to be both encouraging
and logical. As DIDAR removes spectra that may contribute to identifications,
but may not contribute in any way to quantification, we would expect
loss at the peptide spectral match level but, at worst, no loss in
quantitative accuracy.
Conclusions
We have described the
application of a rapid, lightweight Python
tool for the quality assessment and filtering of single cell proteomics
data. When applied in this manner, DIDAR can flag both entire LCMS
runs that experienced technical issues for further evaluation or 
removal from analysis. In addition, DIDAR can generate new input files
that contain only data meeting user required minimum cutoffs. While
peptide spectral match level data is lost following filtering, this
appears to have minimal effects on the final processed data, as the
determinant of peptide and protein existence in this workflow is the
presence of reporter ion signal from each cell. Future directions
for this work include automating DIDAR as a step in our data analysis
pipeline through the execution in the HyStar interface. Furthermore,
today the TIMSTOF instruments must collect two MS/MS scans for each
reporter ion experiment as the time-of-flight effect out of the quadrupole
can not be neutralized to allow both low and high mass ions to be
collected simultaneously. Current work in the lab to institute DIDAR
filtering in real time may allow significant increases in duty cycle
by allowing the TIMSTOF to only spend time sequencing MS/MS spectra
which possess a user specified number of single cell reporter ions,
similar to a recently described glycoproteomics workflow.
20
